joinspy

keys that look identical but aren’t

joinspy checks the key columns of two tables before they are joined and reports the values that will not match, such as keys with a trailing space, a different case or an invisible Unicode character.

R compares join keys byte by byte, so "B " and "B" are different keys and the join drops the row without a warning. The diagnostic report names each affected value, says why it fails to match and predicts the row count of every join type. You can then preview the repairs, apply them, or copy the generated code into your own script. joinspy supports:

  • Repairing keys. join_repair() trims whitespace, standardises case and removes invisible characters, with dry_run = TRUE to preview the changes. suggest_repairs() prints the same fixes as R code.
  • Predicting the result size. The report gives the row count of the inner, left, right and full join from the key multiplicities, so a many-to-many key shows up before the join multiplies the rows.
  • Declaring the relationship of the keys. join_strict() joins only when the keys hold the declared relationship ("1:1", "1:n", "n:1" or "n:m") and stops with an error otherwise.
  • Explaining a join that already ran. join_explain() compares the row count of a result with its two inputs and lists the keys that had no match.
  • Three join engines. Tibbles are joined with dplyr, data.tables with data.table and plain data frames with base merge(), and the class of the input is kept through diagnosis, repair and join.

Installation 

install.packages("joinspy")

Development version:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/joinspy")

Usage

  1. Check the keys of the two tables with join_spy().
  2. Fix whitespace, case and invisible characters with join_repair().
  3. Join the repaired tables with left_join_spy() or one of the other wrappers, which run the same check and attach the report to the result.

join_spy() takes two data frames, tibbles or data.tables and the key columns in by: the shared column names, or a named vector such as c("id" = "customer_id") when the names differ.

library(joinspy)

orders <- data.frame(
  id     = c("A", "B ", "c", "D"),
  amount = c(100, 200, 300, 400)
)
customers <- data.frame(
  id   = c("A", "B", "C", "E"),
  name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Carol", "Eve")
)
join_spy(orders, customers, by = "id")
#> 
#> ── Join Diagnostic Report ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Join columns: id
#> 
#> ── Table Summary ──
#> 
#> Left table: Rows: 4 Unique keys: 4 Duplicate keys: 0 NA keys: 0
#> Right table: Rows: 4 Unique keys: 4 Duplicate keys: 0 NA keys: 0
#> 
#> ── Match Analysis ──
#> 
#> Keys in both: 1
#> Keys only in left: 3
#> Keys only in right: 3
#> Match rate (left): "25%"
#> 
#> ── Issues Detected ──
#> 
#> ! Left column 'id' has 1 value(s) with leading/trailing whitespace
#> ! 1 key(s) would match if case-insensitive (e.g., 'c' vs 'C')
#> 
#> ── Expected Row Counts ──
#> 
#> inner_join: 1
#> left_join: 4
#> right_join: 4
#> full_join: 7

Only "A" matches as written. "B " carries a trailing space and "c" differs from "C" in case, so each would match after a repair. "D" has no counterpart in customers and stays unmatched whatever is repaired.

fixed <- join_repair(orders, customers, by = "id", standardize_case = "upper")
#> ✔ Repaired 2 value(s)
joined <- left_join_spy(fixed$x, fixed$y, by = "id", .quiet = TRUE)
joined
#>   id amount  name
#> 1  A    100 Alice
#> 2  B    200   Bob
#> 3  C    300 Carol
#> 4  D    400  <NA>

Three of the four orders now find their customer, and order "D" keeps an NA name. last_report() returns the report of the most recent join.

What the report checks

Each key column is checked for:

  • leading and trailing whitespace;
  • values that differ between the two tables only in case;
  • invisible Unicode characters (zero-width spaces, byte order marks, non-breaking spaces) and mixed encodings;
  • empty strings, which match each other in a join while NA does not;
  • type and factor-level mismatches between the two tables;
  • floating-point keys that may not compare equal;
  • near matches within a Levenshtein distance of two, which may be typos.

Why Your Keys Don’t Match shows each case at the byte level, and Common Join Problems gives the fix for each.

Declaring the relationship of the keys

A join that should attach one customer to each order can multiply rows when a key repeats. join_strict() takes the expected relationship and stops before joining when the data breaks it:

items <- data.frame(id = c("A", "A", "B"), qty = c(2, 1, 5))
join_strict(customers, items, by = "id", expect = "1:1")
#> Error in `join_strict()`:
#> ! Cardinality violation: expected "1:1" but found "1:n".
#> ℹ Left duplicates: 0, right duplicates: 1.

detect_cardinality() reports the relationship the keys actually have. Joins in Production uses these checks as gates in a pipeline, with logged reports.

Explaining a join that already ran

join_explain() takes a result and the two tables it came from, and accounts for its row count:

result <- merge(orders, customers, by = "id", all.x = TRUE)
join_explain(result, orders, customers, by = "id", type = "left")
#> 
#> ── Join Explanation ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 
#> ── Row Counts ──
#> 
#> Left table (x): 4 rows
#> Right table (y): 4 rows
#> Result: 4 rows
#> ✔ Result has same row count as left table
#> 
#> ── Why the row count changed ──
#> 
#> ℹ 3 left key(s) have no match in right table

Related packages

Package Focus
dplyr 1.1+ Cardinality checks via the relationship argument
powerjoin Configurable join checks and key preprocessing
joyn Per-row match-status reporting variable
tidylog Logs row count changes after joins

joinspy works on the key values themselves: it names the values that fail to match, gives the reason and can repair them.
